After leaving the Capitol at 4:38 in the morning, I showed up to this Juneteenth celebration and was immediately reminded of exactly WHY I do this work. The energy in that room was electric, powerful women, powerful voices, powerful community. All gathered together to honor something bigger than any one of us. Juneteenth is a celebration. But it is also a call to action. Our ancestors earned this joy. Now it is our job to build the world they deserved.  #Juneteenth #BlackWomenLead #QuantáForAZ #LD26 #JuneteenthCelebration

Juneteenth is not just a celebration of freedom. It is a reminder that the work of liberation is never finished the moment it is declared; it has to be ENFORCED. It has to be protected. It has to be fought for, generation after generation.

On June 19th, 1865 - two years after the Emancipation Proclamation - soldiers arrived in Texas with the news that the Civil War had ended and that enslaved people were finally free. That day became known as Juneteenth, and it stands as a nationally celebrated commemoration of the end of slavery in the United States.  This week, we’re taking a moment to reflect on what freedom really means. Noting that it took two years for the Emancipation Proclamation to be effectively enforced reminds us that freedom is not just a historical milestone but an ongoing pursuit. It has to be fought for, generation after generation. Every generation should also protect the work of the previous one, ensuring that their efforts are recognized and continue to build our communities and future.

I had the privilege of attending the 2026 Fair Tax Summit, a national convening of state legislators, policy advocates, and progressive leaders united around one powerful principle: the wealthy and corporations must pay their fair share, and we have the receipts to prove it is possible. The summit brought together lawmakers from across the country to share strategies, celebrate wins, and build the political will to make our tax systems work for working people instead of the ultra-rich. And the momentum is REAL. States across the nation are making bold moves: - Washington, Maine, and Hawaii all passed millionaires’ taxes this session   - Rhode Island is on the verge of passing one   - New York passed a luxury second home tax   - Illinois and Utah passed digital ad taxes   - Right here in Arizona, we passed a 3-year moratorium on data center tax exemptions, a hard-fought win that protects our communities from subsidizing billion-dollar corporations at the expense of our power grid and water supply   - And more than a dozen states decoupled from federal tax giveaways that would have drained state revenues Billions in tax revenue defended. That is what collective action looks like. I was honored to be in the room alongside incredible colleagues fighting this same fight, including Senator Annalise Ortiz and Senator Kiana Maria Sears, two powerhouse Arizona legislators who show up every single day for economic justice and working families. Having Arizona representation at this summit matters. The policies being shaped in rooms like this one will directly impact the people of LD 26, and I am making sure our community’s voice is at that table. Because here is the truth: when billionaires and corporations pay their fair share, we can fully fund our schools, fix our roads, expand healthcare access, and build the kind of Arizona that works for everyone, not just those at the top. That is not radical. That is basic math. And it is exactly what I am fighting for every single day.

I went back to therapy because I’m learning, in practice, one way to fight depression is through expression. It had been more than six months. I’ve been in one of the biggest slumps I’ve had since my brother died, and in refusing to let myself stay there, I figured I had a lot to catch up on. When I’m hurting, my instinct is usually the opposite. Unplug, disconnect, disappear. Stay busy enough that I don’t have to deal. And I’ve gotten pretty good at it.  But there’s something deeply sad about realizing how much of my life i’ve lost to not allowing myself to feel it. It doesn’t leave much room for everything else. At some point, “protecting yourself” starts looking a lot like disconnecting yourself from your own life. There’s something to be learned from otherwise. So instead, I talked. I cried. I laughed. I let myself say things out loud that had mostly been living in my head. And then I decided to share some of it here. One thing I’ve learned from working alongside public officials, and then campaigning to be one, is just how much of our lives we’re willing to share publicly. But I don’t want vulnerability to only be something I share once it’s been curated. In my case, that has almost always meant waiting until I’ve survived something, processed it, packaged it neatly, and found the lesson. Sometimes vulnerability is just letting yourself be seen while you’re still figuring it out. And I can confidently say we’re all figuring something out. No lesson or conclusion yet. Just trying something different this time. So, join me. Get your ass back to therapy and deal with it, girlie. 🫶🏽

For as long as I can remember, I’ve set my sights on things bigger than I ever imagined I’d have the opportunity to do, and I’ve been fortunate enough to realize some of them. But for the first time in over five years, there’s been enough stillness to think about what it’s all cost me. I’ve worked hard and remain incredibly grateful. But I think when you’re constantly working toward something, it becomes easy to convince yourself that whatever you put aside today can be made up for tomorrow. That once you’ve reached the next milestone, there will finally be time for everything and everyone you’ve been meaning to get back to. The trouble is, life keeps happening whether you’re paying attention to it or not. I’ve missed moments, neglected relationships, and sometimes treated my own well-being as something I could get around to later. I don’t think every sacrifice was necessary, and I certainly don’t think each was worth it. That’s been a difficult thing to reconcile with how proud I am of what I’ve accomplished. For years, so much of my life has revolved around the next opportunity to be of service. It’s one of the things that brings me the greatest fulfillment, and I don’t see that changing. But somewhere along the way, I got used to treating everything else as something that could wait. And I’m realizing how much life happens in the meantime, and how much that mindset has taken a toll. So I’m trying to give those parts of my life the attention they deserve, too. This month, beyond work, I’ve reached new milestones at the gym, I’m moving into a new home, and I’ve gotten back into school. I’m looking forward to reconnecting with myself and the people I love in the next. 🖤

300+ books and a whole lot of stops around Tucson later! 📚❤️ In 2025, just 33% of third graders in Pima County met proficiency standards in English Language Arts. That’s only one in three children, and a reminder of how much work Arizona has ahead to ensure kids have the opportunity to become confident readers. Thankfully, Tucson has some incredible people and organizations doing that work every day. From Little Free Library volunteers making books accessible in our neighborhoods to Make Way for Books and Literacy Connects helping children and families develop lifelong literacy skills, there’s a lot of good happening in our community. I spent some time distributing over 300 books to Little Free Libraries across Tucson, and it reminded me how something as simple as sharing a book can help make reading more accessible to someone else. So if you’ve got books sitting on a shelf that you’re ready to part with, consider giving them another life. You can find a Little Free Library near you at littlefreelibrary.org/map. And if you’re looking to make a bigger difference, consider supporting or volunteering with the organizations working to improve literacy across Southern Arizona. A book you’ve already read might be someone else’s next favorite. 🖤📖

Well… that’s a wrap, at least for now. After six months of committee hearings, floor sessions, meetings, late nights, and more cups of coffee than I’d like to admit, the Legislature is officially on summer recess. This Fourth of July I finally had some time to slow down and just wander through my backyard. It’s been a while since I really stopped to appreciate everything that’s been growing in my own little Jardín Mexicano. My pomegranates, avocado tree, prickly pear, and nopales are all thriving. Even the chickens were out making noise like they own the place. These are the little things the hustle and bustle of commuting to Sacramento usually keeps me from enjoying. I’m especially grateful to be on summer recess and have the chance to simply be home, spend time in the garden, and even swing on the old tree swing for a bit. Sometimes the best moments are the quiet ones. 🌿🇲🇽❤️

It was great spending the Fourth of July with so many community members across Assembly District 15. From parades to local celebrations, it was a wonderful reminder of what brings us together. As we celebrate our nation’s 250th birthday, let’s remember that our freedoms and our democracy aren’t something we can take for granted. There was something so refreshing about experiencing those long northern summer evenings. A quick reminder that even on a fast-paced work trip, it’s worth taking a moment to explore, appreciate a new place, and soak in the little surprises along the way. ☀️🍁 #Edmonton #Canada #LegislativeLife #SummerEvenings #WorkTrip

Thursday evening in San Francisco with our next Governor. Always an honor to be in the room, exchange ideas, and talk about the policies that can move California forward. So, we gathered in the Members’ Lounge for some much-needed comfort food. ❤️ Grateful to our colleague from San Diego for treating us to an amazing meal and giving us a chance to pause, recharge, and enjoy some good food and even better company!

Here we go closing out Legislative Session 2026! ❤️ Roll call to establish a quorum and record attendance! Today, on the green carpet, I get to spend my final day in Sacramento with my son as my floor guest. A pretty special way to close out session and an unforgettable summer together at the Capitol. ❤️🏛️

Sometimes you just have to unplug midweek, lace up, and run away from the chaos for a little while! 😂👟 Early-morning 5-mile adventure to recharge, recalibrate, and remind myself that coffee isn’t the only way to survive the week! ☕️🏃🏻‍♀️✨
Grateful for this long weekend with no commitments just time to decompress from Sacramento and recalibrate for the work ahead in the district. 🌿☀️
This morning, I ventured beyond my usual neighborhood walk and made it all the way to the downtown Martinez waterfront! 🌊👟☀️
Nothing fancy just a cool evening, a good walk, and a little time to decompress. Exactly what I needed.

I didn’t realize just how much I missed this. 🌞 After nine months of Capitol life recycled air, fluorescent lights, freezing air-conditioning, long days, and very little time to just be outside it feels SO good to be home and feel the sunshine on my face again. ☀️
Sunday morning cemetery vibes. ⚰️🌿 My morning run took me to a different part of Martinez along the Carquinez Strait, where two of our historic cemeteries sit tucked into the hillside.

Five days post-legislative session and SO happy to be back in the district! ❤️ Time to get back into consistent, healthy routines movement, exercise, and cardio. Sacramento may have stolen some of my daily fitness routine, so let’s see what’s left! 😂

Today, I’m especially grateful for the generations of union members who fought for fair wages, safer workplaces, benefits, and a stronger voice for working people. Thank you to all the workers who keep our communities going. ✊🏽
Out before 7 AM, beating the heat, catching some sunshine, and getting a little self-care in before the people’s work! ☀️ Back in the district, ready to work hard just trying not to lose a lung! 😂🫁
Today in my district I got to visit a local family-owned McDonald’s, meet the amazing people who keep it running, and hear about the challenges of operating a business in California.

Today I joined the Clayton community for a 9/11 remembrance ceremony. It’s hard to imagine that it’s been 25 years. I still remember where I was that morning and how our country changed forever. I’m grateful to our local first responders and to everyone who continues to come together each year to honor the lives lost and the heroes who stepped forward. We remember. We honor. We will never forget. 🇺🇸

Today, in my hometown Martinez, we came together for a moment of silence, as I have done almost every year. It’s truly heartwarming to see our gathering grow each year. For those of us who remember, we carry that day with us. And for those who don’t, it’s up to us to share what we remember, honor those we lost, and make sure their stories are never forgotten. 🇺🇸

REPOST! AB 2664 is on Governor Newsom's desk, waiting his signature. We have to tell him to veto this bill.  This bill seeks to undermine our right to protest. This bill makes it a criminal offense to protest or pass out political material within 100 feet of a place of worship, including public spaces like sidewalks and private property. Let me be clear: people should absolutely have the right to practice their faith in peace. However, this bill does not seek to accomplish that. Its sole purpose is to protect evangelical churches and synagogues holding fundraisers for the IDF and events promoting the sales of stolen Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank. Bills like this also have a number of unintended but related negative consequences - for instance, preventing a community’s ability to protest the promotion of hate against our LGBTQAI+ neighbors, if a church were to hold such an event. Places of worship have long been important locations for community organizing, with one prime example being a part of the history of Black Liberation. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. began his fight for civil rights by handing out materials in front of churches.

I spent about a year trying to figure out where to put money before I understood what was actually broken. Everyone kept saying awareness. More awareness, more training, more funding. But the people I needed to reach had been taught that calling for help meant getting arrested. Some of them had been bought by someone with a badge. Awareness doesn't touch that. What was missing was a phone number they'd trust. So we built one, and I answered it for eleven years. Most problems are like this. The obvious fix isn't aimed at the real cause.

The question I got asked over and over again in eleven years: "How did nobody see it?" Somebody almost always did. A mom noticed the new presents. A coach noticed the older boyfriend. A friend noticed the wall going up. Each person explained away their one piece, and nobody ever put the pieces together. That's why the video says three together, not one alone. One sign is a Tuesday. Three is a pattern. And a parent who spots a pattern beats every system I've ever worked with, including mine. You don't need training to be that one adult. You need the frame, and the willingness to have an awkward conversation a week too early instead of a year too late. #Awareness #CommunitySupport #ParentingWisdom #EarlyIntervention #BeTheOne

caption: Andy Boesenecker claims he’s fighting for small business. His record shows the opposite: He was the lead House sponsor of HB26-1001 (the HOME Act). This law forces local governments (including Fort Collins) to fast-track housing projects on public and nonprofit land with very little community input or local review. → This is the opposite of protecting local control and local business environments. It overrides local zoning and can strain roads, parking, and infrastructure that small businesses rely on. He supported (and the Democratic majority passed) HB25B-1005, the elimination of the vendor fee that small retailers were allowed to keep as compensation for collecting and remitting state sales tax. → Starting in 2026, many small retailers lost that small but real offset. This is a direct cost increase on the exact businesses he claims to champion. In the 2025 special session he was a primary sponsor of HB25-S1003,  the bill that ended the home-office/regional-office premium tax reduction for insurers. → This raised taxes on companies that employ people in Colorado; higher costs get passed along. He strongly backed HB26-1223, the bill that removed the state sales-tax exemption on downloadable and cloud-based software. → Small businesses and entrepreneurs now pay sales tax on the software tools they use every day (accounting, design, point-of-sale, etc.). I’ll cut the taxes, fees, and red tape that are crushing Fort Collins entrepreneurs. We don't need any more "representatives" that don't actually serve and enhance the lives of their voters. Help me replace him. I want to take a minute to explain the difference between hard money, soft money, and dark money in political advertising—and why it matters when you’re deciding where your information is coming from. Hard money is the money my campaign raises and spends directly to get my message out to our community. Soft money is money spent independently by outside groups with their own interests. Those groups may spend money supporting me or opposing me because they believe I will—or won’t—advance the issues they care about. They are independent from my campaign, and they cannot legally coordinate their spending with us. Dark money is different because the original sources funding the political spending may not be publicly disclosed. That can make it difficult for voters to know who is ultimately behind a message or why they are paying to put it in front of you. That’s why I encourage everyone: look at the disclaimer. Ask who paid for the ad. Understand where your information is coming from. You deserve to know who is trying to influence your opinion. I also want to address my career as a criminal justice attorney and public defender. In the United States, every person accused of a crime is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. Every person is entitled to a defense, and our justice system depends on attorneys who make sure the government follows the Constitution and obeys the law. That’s what I’ve done throughout my career: hold government accountable and defend people’s rights. And that’s the experience I’ll bring to the State Senate—standing up for Pueblo’s interests and making sure our community has a strong advocate at the Capitol.

In my Orlando Sentinel interview, I was asked: Are Florida elections secure? My answer is yes, our elections are secure. But we also need to make our elections more fair and equitable. Everyone deserves the opportunity to participate in our democracy. That means making sure voters have meaningful opportunities to cast their ballots around their work, family, and other responsibilities. We also need accountability for so-called ghost candidates and practices that can affect the choices available to voters. Our elections should be secure, accessible, and representative of the people they serve. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my campaign and my positions.

In my Orlando Sentinel interview, I was asked about my stance on data centers. My answer is clear: I do not believe data centers have a place here in Florida. This is an issue that should bring people together across the political spectrum. Protecting our environment, our water, and the aquifer we all depend on should not be a partisan issue. Florida’s natural resources are limited, and we need to make sure our communities have enough clean water for generations to come. I’m calling on Floridians from every political background to come together, protect our environment and our water, and say no to data centers. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my position.

In my Orlando Sentinel interview, I was asked: What should the state do about the Hope Florida scandal? My answer is clear: we need a criminal investigation into who was responsible. A state grand jury found that $10 million from a Medicaid settlement was misappropriated and ultimately routed through nonprofits into political committees. The grand jury found insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges, but that does not mean we should stop asking questions or demanding accountability. That money came from a Medicaid settlement involving a program that serves vulnerable Floridians. Taxpayer dollars should never be diverted for political purposes. We also need serious accountability when it comes to the state's management of public education funding and school voucher programs. When hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars are involved, Floridians deserve transparency, oversight, and answers. We need leadership that follows the money, investigates wrongdoing, and makes sure taxpayer dollars are used for the people they were intended to serve. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my campaign and my commitment to fighting corruption.

In my Orlando Sentinel interview, I was asked what I think about the state legislature’s war on D.E.I. My answer is simple: stay out of local government affairs. I believe in home rule and the right of locally elected governments to make decisions that reflect the communities they represent. That includes allowing local governments to host parades, cultural awareness events, and heritage celebrations without Tallahassee weaponizing state power to interfere with local decision-making. Our communities are diverse, and local governments should have the freedom to celebrate and bring people together without unnecessary state interference. I will fight to protect home rule and keep decisions about our communities where they belong: with the people who live here and the local governments they elect. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my positions.

Preemption is stripping away local control and weakening home rule across Florida. One example is the fight over the Rural Boundary. In Seminole County, voters have repeatedly made their position clear about protecting rural and natural lands. In 2024, 82% of voters approved a charter amendment requiring a supermajority vote to remove property from the county’s Rural Area. Now, state-level proposals are challenging the ability of local communities to make these decisions for themselves. Seminole County has also had to pause its Rural Enclaves Study because state law restricts counties from adopting certain land-use regulations that go beyond state requirements. I believe decisions about our communities should be made by the people who live here and the local governments they elect, not dictated by Tallahassee. We need to protect home rule, preserve the Rural Boundary, concentrate responsible growth where infrastructure already exists, and protect the wildlife and natural lands that make Central Florida special. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my position and why protecting local control matters.

In my Orlando Sentinel interview, I was asked about Amendment 3, the property tax proposal on the 2026 ballot. I’ve said I would vote NO because I’m concerned about what significant reductions in local property tax revenue could mean for the parks, local programs, sports programs, and services that families rely on. The proposal would exempt the first $250,000 of homestead value from certain local taxes and restrict how local governments can use remaining property tax revenue. I believe we should pursue property tax relief in a way that protects working families while asking more from people who own second and third homes. My goal is to lower the tax burden for lower-income working families in their primary home without undermining the ability of local governments to provide essential services. We need to organize around solutions that provide meaningful affordability relief while protecting local communities and home rule. Visit my website at blockfor36.com to learn more about my position.

No family should have to face a crisis like that while also worrying about whether they can afford the healthcare they need. This is part of Florida’s affordability crisis, and we need to change it now. I will fight to expand access to healthcare and make sure working families have the coverage they need when they need it.
